In June 1865 Russian troops under General Mikhail Chernyayev stormed Tashkent, the largest city in Central Asia, then held by the Khanate of Kokand. Chernyayev attacked with a small force and without clear orders; his success was approved after the fact.

Tashkent became the capital of the new Governorate-General of Turkestan in 1867, under Konstantin von Kaufmann. From there Russia took the Uzbek khanates one by one: Bukhara became a protectorate after losing Samarkand in 1868, Khiva fell in 1873, and Kokand was abolished in 1876. The conquest ended with the massacre of Turkmen defenders at Geok Tepe in 1881.

Russia wanted cotton, trade and a secure frontier, and its advance alarmed the British in India, sharpening the rivalry known as the Great Game. A Russian new town grew up beside the old city. Tashkent stayed the centre of Russian and Soviet rule in the region and is now the capital of Uzbekistan.
